articles.title: Plant Orbiter: 3D Plant Reconstruction and Generation with Video Diffusion Orbit Cameras and 3D Gaussian Splatting
articles.summary: Modern digital phenotyping pipelines require the precise measurement of a range of 3D morphological plant traits. The accurate, high throughput acquisition of these traits helps breeders and researchers accelerate the development of new varieties, techniques and products. Recent advances in 3D technologies have enabled a rapid transition from 2D to 3D pipelines, but high throughput acquisition of digital 3D twins of plants remains a significant challenge due to complex morphology, thin structures and occlusions. In this paper we present Plant Orbiter, a new approach to generating 3D plants that leverages recent advances in video diffusion to produce high quality 3D Gaussian Splats of plants from a single image. We show that our method more accurately recreates plant morphology than other state-of-the-art methods, achieving the highest 3D F-score against all baselines, while being more practical for high throughput pipelines due to easier alignment and reduced cost of camera placement.
articles.author: Michael P. Pound

articles.title: Towards Reconstructing and Recognizing Objects behind Fragmented Occlusion using Video
articles.summary: Perceiving objects through fragmented occlusions, such as foliage, is a natural capability of the human visual system but remains a fundamental challenge for computer vision. This work addresses the problem of object reconstruction, or de-occlusion, in the presence of high-density, fragmented occlusions. We propose a reconstruction framework that operates on a sequence of grayscale images of a moving object, acquired by a single camera, either stationary or in motion. The algorithm estimates the object's relative positions across frames by jointly registering the images and optimizing the alignment parameters to maximize the contrast of their average, referred to as the integrated image. This integrated image serves as the reconstructed representation of the object. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real video sequences demonstrate the feasibility of accurate reconstruction under occlusion densities exceeding 90%. articles.title: I benchmarked TimesFM 3.0, Chronos-2 and Toto 2.0 on market time series. None beat simple baseline. [P]
articles.summary: I may be naive, but I've been curious whether the recent wave of time-series foundation models can actually extract useful predictive signals from financial markets. Models like Google's TimesFM 3.0, Amazon's Chronos-2, and Datadog's Toto 2.0 are impressive general-purpose forecasters from the first sight. But stock prices are difficult to predict, so I wanted to see how these models perform against very simple baselines. I ran a series of zero-shot experiments on 24 US stocks and ETFs, including daily and intraday data, and compared their predictions against naive forecasting strategies and also simulated random walks. TL;DR none of the three models showed any meaningful predictive power for stock price movements in this setup.
